paragraphs: Bilevel optimization involves two linked optimization problems: the decision made at the upper level depends on the solution found at the lower level. This paper develops a framework for cases where both sets of variables must lie on Riemannian manifolds. These geometric constraints shape how the optimization process can move and how derivatives are defined.

A central contribution concerns hypergradients, which describe how changing an upper-level variable affects the objective through the lower-level problem. The authors introduce several ways to estimate these quantities on manifolds and analyze their estimation errors. They also study convergence and computational complexity for a hypergradient descent algorithm that operates within this geometric setting.

The framework also covers stochastic bilevel optimization and general retractions, which provide a way to perform updates on a manifold. Applications demonstrate its effectiveness. The contribution brings gradient estimation, algorithm design, and theoretical analysis together, providing a framework for nested optimization problems whose variables must respect geometric constraints at both levels.
neurips-2024-a-framework-for-bilevel-opt.tldr: The paper develops and analyzes methods for bilevel optimization when both levels have variables constrained to Riemannian manifolds.

paragraphs: Where do a transformer's algorithmic abilities come from? Training can produce recognizable procedures for tasks such as arithmetic and recall, but some useful computation might already exist in the randomly initialized network. This paper investigates that possibility by restricting which parts of the model can learn from examples.

The researchers optimize only the embedding layers while keeping the randomly initialized transformer fixed. This setup lets training choose an encoding that makes existing computations accessible. Consequently, the experiment tests which input-to-output mappings the random network can support through a suitable representation, without changing its internal transformer parameters to build a new procedure.

The resulting models perform modular arithmetic, associative recall both in weights and in context, decimal addition, and parenthesis balancing. They also exhibit some aspects of natural-language generation. These findings indicate that some algorithmic capabilities are accessible before the transformer itself is trained. The qualification matters: learned embeddings and appropriately structured inputs play a central role in exposing those capabilities.
neurips-2024-algorithmic-capabilities-of.tldr: Randomly initialized transformers can support several algorithmic tasks when only their embedding layers are trained.

paragraphs: Many detectors assess whether text was generated by a language model by measuring how easily a model predicts each next token. BiScope adds a second signal: the extent to which the model's output scores retain information about nearby preceding tokens. The paper finds that this backward-looking information also helps distinguish generated text.

For each relevant output, the method computes cross-entropy losses against two targets: the token used for forward prediction and the immediately preceding input token. It then summarizes these losses into statistics and trains a classifier to make the detection decision. This combines evidence about continuation prediction with evidence about preceding-token memorization.

The evaluation covers text from five commercial language models across five datasets containing natural language and code. BiScope outperforms six comparison methods, reports an average F1 score above 0.95, and exceeds the strongest noncommercial methods by more than 0.30 F1. It also surpasses GPTZero in the reported evaluation. These results support using both directions of evidence for detection across the tested settings.
neurips-2024-biscope-ai-generated-text-d.tldr: BiScope detects generated text using both next-token prediction losses and evidence that model outputs retain preceding tokens.

paragraphs: Human comparisons support tasks such as learning rankings and aligning language models, yet subjective judgments often cannot be checked against an objectively correct answer. This paper asks how payments can encourage rational participants to report their comparisons truthfully. Its mechanisms use bonuses and penalties, with each participant evaluating and reporting just one pair.

The comparison mechanism relies on strong stochastic transitivity, a structural assumption about comparison data. Under this structure, truthful reporting forms a strict Bayesian Nash equilibrium: when others report truthfully, a participant has a strict incentive to do the same. Truthful reporting also produces the highest payment among symmetric equilibria, strengthening the incentive beyond simply making honesty an equilibrium.

The authors extend the payment idea to networked data whose private signals follow Ising models. They also establish necessary and sufficient conditions for the bonus-penalty payment to make truth-telling a strict Bayesian Nash equilibrium. Experiments on two real-world datasets support the theoretical findings. The guarantees concern incentives under the stated signal structures and equilibrium concepts.
neurips-2024-carrot-and-stick-eliciting-.tldr: Bonus-penalty mechanisms encourage truthful comparison reports under stated structural assumptions and extend to certain networked signals.

paragraphs: Snapshot compressive imaging reconstruction models are often trained for one carefully calibrated hardware setup. Their performance can suffer when the hardware changes, making it difficult to reuse a model across different systems. Collecting data from every system for centralized training creates additional problems because institutions face privacy concerns and use heterogeneous hardware.

FedHP addresses this through federated learning with a hardware-conditioned prompter. The prompter learns to align differences in the data distributions produced by different hardware configurations, including coded apertures. This targets a source of disagreement in the input data itself. The paper contrasts this approach with gradient corrections, which address differences during optimization without resolving that underlying input inconsistency.

Experiments show that FedHP adapts a pretrained model to multiple hardware configurations and improves on prevalent federated learning frameworks by 0.35 dB in challenging heterogeneous settings. The authors also construct a spectral imaging dataset using multiple practical systems. Together, these contributions connect cooperative model adaptation with the hardware differences encountered across actual imaging platforms.
neurips-2024-cooperative-hardware-prompt.tldr: FedHP uses hardware-conditioned prompts in federated learning to adapt imaging reconstruction models across heterogeneous hardware.

paragraphs: Learning from individual preference pairs does not by itself establish that preferred responses have better rewards across their full distribution. Alignment via Optimal Transport, or AOT, targets that broader relationship. It works with unpaired positive and negative preference samples, seeking first-order stochastic dominance of the positive reward distribution over the negative one.

The authors introduce a convex relaxation of this dominance requirement and express it as an optimal transport problem with a smooth, convex cost. Because the transport problem is one-dimensional, its empirical solution can be obtained by sorting. The resulting fine-tuning objective penalizes violations of the desired distributional ordering, giving a practical training procedure for the broader alignment target.

The paper also analyzes sample complexity through the transport problem's dual formulation and establishes convergence at the parametric rate. Across multiple alignment datasets and language models, the authors report state-of-the-art results within the 7B model family on Open LLM Benchmarks and AlpacaEval. These findings support distribution-level preference objectives as a useful approach to language-model fine-tuning.
neurips-2024-distributional-preference-a.tldr: AOT fine-tunes language models with an efficiently computed transport objective that penalizes undesirable ordering of positive and negative reward distributions.

paragraphs: Federated learning must often operate with devices that connect intermittently. Availability can differ across clients and change over time, especially when clients move or deployment conditions are uncertain. This paper studies both effects together and illustrates how they can significantly affect FedAvg, a widely used federated learning algorithm.

The proposed method, FedAWE, compensates for computations missed while a client is unavailable. It does so with only constant additional memory and computation relative to standard FedAvg. A second component spreads local updates evenly through the system using implicit gossiping. The method does not require knowledge of the changing dynamics that govern client availability.

The authors show convergence to a stationary point for nonconvex objectives and establish a linear speedup property. A stationary-point result describes a convergence target without asserting that the algorithm reaches a global optimum. Experiments on real-world datasets with varied availability dynamics support the analysis. The contribution combines adaptation to unreliable participation with limited added computational and memory demands.
neurips-2024-efficient-federated-learnin.tldr: FedAWE handles unequal and changing client availability through missed-computation compensation and implicit gossiping with constant added overhead.

paragraphs: In recommendation and advertising data, missing observations often reflect a selective collection process. Methods that correct this selection can become unstable when propensity scores, which describe observation probabilities, approach zero. This paper examines why pursuing unbiased estimates in that setting can produce unbounded variance and unbounded generalization guarantees.

The authors first analyze limitations of regularization and then establish a broader connection between unbiasedness and unbounded variance in the setting they study. Their response is to optimize bias and variance quantitatively together. They introduce a dynamic framework that selects an estimator separately for each user-item pair according to a predefined objective.

This pair-specific choice lets the learning process adapt its estimation strategy at a finer level than choosing one estimator for all observations. The paper provides theoretical guarantees that the resulting variances and generalization bounds are reduced and bounded. Extensive experiments support the analysis and the framework's effectiveness, showing the value of explicitly accounting for both sources of estimation error.
neurips-2024-fine-grained-dynamic-framew.tldr: The framework selects estimators for individual user-item pairs to jointly control bias and variance when observations are missing nonrandomly.

paragraphs: Single-cell sequencing destroys the measured cells and captures only a limited set of modalities together. Researchers therefore need ways to align cells across measurements. Optimal transport offers a framework for this task, but traditional discrete solvers face scalability, privacy, and prediction challenges when applied to previously unseen samples.

GENOT uses flow matching to learn stochastic transport maps, allowing a source cell representation to have a distribution of possible destinations. The approach permits arbitrary cost functions and relaxes mass conservation constraints. It also incorporates quadratic solvers for the Gromov-Wasserstein and fused Gromov-Wasserstein problems, broadening the types of alignment the framework can handle.

The authors demonstrate the method in studies of cell development, cellular responses to drugs, and translation between measurement modalities. These applications support its versatility and robustness across several biological alignment tasks. The significance lies in combining multiple forms of transport flexibility within one neural framework. The abstract presents improved therapeutic strategies as a potential downstream benefit of this modeling capability.
neurips-2024-genot-entropic-gromov-wasse.tldr: GENOT uses flow matching to learn flexible stochastic transport plans for aligning single-cell data across biological conditions and measurement modalities.

paragraphs: Long-tailed recognition involves classes with very different amounts of training data. Visual prompt tuning can use pretrained knowledge effectively, yet its generalization on rare classes remains unsatisfactory. This paper introduces Gaussian neighborhood minimization prompt tuning, or GNM-PT, to improve optimization in that setting, with benefits reported across both frequent and rare classes.

The method introduces a Gaussian neighborhood loss that tightly upper-bounds the loss over the data distribution. During each update, it seeks a descent direction within a random neighborhood of parameters that is independent of the input samples. This encourages a flatter loss landscape, a property the paper associates with better generalization.

The authors report improved generalization across all classes alongside reduced computational overhead. Classification accuracies reach 90.3% on CIFAR100-LT with imbalance ratio 100, 76.5% on iNaturalist 2018, and 50.1% on Places-LT, which the paper reports as state of the art. These results support changing the prompt optimization strategy as a way to improve recognition under substantial class imbalance.
neurips-2024-improving-visual-prompt-tun.tldr: GNM-PT improves visual prompt tuning for imbalanced recognition by optimizing a Gaussian parameter-neighborhood loss.

paragraphs: Self-supervised vision methods often build in assumptions about which transformations should leave a representation unchanged or change it predictably. Those assumptions can make representations fragile when downstream tasks require different behavior. ContextSSL addresses this by learning a general representation whose treatment of transformations can adapt using a small number of contextual examples.

The approach draws on world models and uses a memory of states, actions, and future states. Here, an action is a transformation, while the states represent the input before and after that transformation. ContextSSL learns equivariance across the transformations: representations capture their effects. Context then guides how the model adapts to the symmetries relevant to a particular task.

This design aims to retain relevant features while allowing task-specific invariance or equivariance to emerge from context. The authors report significant improvements over existing methods on tasks involving equivariance, supported by qualitative and quantitative evaluations. The findings support using contextual information to make learned representations more adaptable to differing transformation requirements.
neurips-2024-in-context-symmetries-self-.tldr: ContextSSL learns transformation-aware visual representations that adapt to task-specific symmetries using a few contextual examples.

paragraphs: Safety alignment can be weakened when a language model is fine-tuned on user data containing harmful examples. This paper shows that separating fine-tuning into two optimization states, one for alignment data and one for user data, can mitigate that effect. However, this basic approach becomes unstable when too few steps are allocated to alignment.

The authors' statistical analysis identifies excessive drift around the points where optimization switches between states as a probable explanation for the instability. Lisa adds a proximal term that constrains each state's drift. This directly addresses the suspected mechanism while preserving the separation between learning from alignment data and learning from the user's task data.

Convergence analysis supports the proximal term and identifies a sufficiently large proximal factor as necessary for the convergence guarantee. On four downstream fine-tuning tasks, Lisa substantially improves alignment while maintaining accuracy on user tasks. These findings support controlling movement between the two optimization states as a practical defense against harmful fine-tuning in the evaluated settings.
neurips-2024-lisa-lazy-safety-alignment-.tldr: Lisa constrains drift between alignment and user-task optimization states to improve safety during potentially harmful fine-tuning.

paragraphs: This paper asks exactly which graph properties recurrent graph neural networks can express, distinguishing networks that use floating-point numbers from those using mathematical real numbers. It answers through logical characterizations: formal languages that match the networks' expressive abilities. Such matches describe what these models can represent at a structural level.

For floating-point networks, the matching language is a rule-based modal logic with counting, under natural assumptions about floating-point arithmetic. For networks using reals, the characterization uses an infinitary modal logic with counting. Both are exact characterizations in the recurrent setting without restricting the comparison to properties from a separate background logic.

The distinction changes when attention is restricted to properties expressible in monadic second-order logic. For that class, recurrent networks with floats and reals are equally expressive, and a finitary rule-based logic characterizes both. In general, however, floats are less expressive than reals. The authors also characterize both kinds of networks through distributed automata, connecting the results to distributed computation.
neurips-2024-logical-characterizations-o.tldr: Exact logical characterizations show when recurrent graph neural networks using floats and reals share expressive power and when they differ.

paragraphs: Continuous normalizing flows learn a probability path from a reference distribution to a target distribution using a neural vector field. This paper adapts flow matching, a method for training these flows, to probabilistic inference. Its central idea is to connect learning the flow with the ongoing process of sampling from the target.

The proposed adaptive MCMC algorithm combines local transitions with nonlocal transitions informed by the learned flow. Samples from the Markov chain continuously update the flow and define the probability path used in its training objective. An adaptive tempering mechanism also helps the sampler discover multiple modes, or separated regions of high probability, in the target distribution.

Under mild assumptions, the authors establish convergence to a local optimum of the flow-matching objective. This guarantee concerns the optimization objective rather than asserting a global optimum. Evaluations on synthetic and real-world examples show performance comparable to other leading methods, often with substantially lower computational cost. The results support jointly adapting a transport model and a sampling process.
neurips-2024-markovian-flow-matching-acc.tldr: Markovian Flow Matching trains a flow from ongoing MCMC samples and uses it to propose efficient nonlocal sampling moves.

paragraphs: Mixture-of-experts transformers can increase their parameter count without a corresponding increase in computation. Widely used designs make discrete expert assignments, while existing continuous alternatives can struggle with performance or autoregressive generation. Mixture of Tokens, or MoT, introduces a continuous architecture intended to retain the scaling benefits of sparse expert models.

Its distinctive operation assigns each expert mixtures of tokens drawn from different examples. This cross-example aggregation replaces conventional assignments with a continuous mechanism. The architecture supports both autoregressive training and generation, making it applicable to language modeling where each output depends on preceding tokens. The paper also introduces transition tuning to demonstrate a close connection between MoT and MoE.

In language pretraining, the authors' best models train three times faster than dense transformers and match the performance of state-of-the-art MoE architectures. These are reported results for the evaluated models. They show that continuous expert architectures can achieve competitive performance while retaining efficient parameter scaling and compatibility with sequential text generation.
neurips-2024-mixture-of-tokens-continuou.tldr: Mixture of Tokens uses continuous cross-example token mixtures to scale expert models while supporting autoregressive language generation.

paragraphs: Behavior cloning learns a policy from demonstrated state-action pairs. This paper studies the teacher's side of that process: how few demonstrations are enough to teach an optimal policy to an entire family of learners? The learners use linear hypothesis classes, and the teacher must choose one dataset that succeeds for the whole family.

The authors develop TIE, a teaching algorithm that achieves the instance-optimal teaching dimension. This means its demonstration count matches the smallest possible count for the particular teaching instance. Optimal dataset size does not automatically make finding that dataset computationally easy: the paper proves that the problem is NP-hard when the action space contains more than two actions.

To address that computational difficulty, the authors also provide an efficient approximation algorithm with a logarithmic guarantee in the number of actions minus one. Experiments compare the approach with several baselines across different teaching environments and demonstrate its effectiveness. The contribution separates the minimum information needed to teach from the computational cost of selecting demonstrations.
neurips-2024-on-the-complexity-of-teachi.tldr: The paper characterizes minimal demonstrations for families of linear behavior-cloning learners and provides an efficient approximation for the NP-hard teaching problem.

paragraphs: Flow-matching generative models learn paths that transport one distribution into another. Straight trajectories are desirable because they support fast numerical integration during inference. Existing approaches to straightening these paths often require iterative flow-matching procedures, which can accumulate training error, or rely on heuristics that solve transport problems within minibatches.

Optimal Flow Matching introduces a theoretically justified route to recovering straight optimal-transport displacements for quadratic transport. Its key design choice is to parameterize the flow-matching vector field using convex functions. This places the desired transport structure within the model's construction and enables recovery through a single flow-matching step in the proposed approach.

The one-step statement concerns the flow-matching procedure used to recover the transport displacement; the abstract does not identify it with a single gradient update or a measured inference speedup. The stated contribution is a direct, theoretically supported approach to straight transport trajectories. The authors also provide an implementation and experiments, connecting the mathematical proposal with an executable method.
neurips-2024-optimal-flow-matching-learn.tldr: Optimal Flow Matching uses convex-function parameterizations to recover straight quadratic optimal-transport displacements in one flow-matching step.

paragraphs: Multiphysics problems involve coupled partial differential equations whose physical variables interact. Neural operators face difficulties with these interactions, complex geometries, and limited high-resolution training data. CoDA-NO addresses these challenges through an architecture that can learn representations of multiple PDE systems within a single model and support self-supervised pretraining.

The model organizes functions into tokens along their codomain, or channel space. It extends positional encoding, self-attention, and normalization to function spaces, bringing these architectural operations into the representation of physical systems. This design provides a common model for learning across different PDE systems before adapting to downstream problems with relatively few examples.

The authors evaluate that potential in few-shot settings involving fluid flow, fluid-structure interactions, and Rayleigh-Bénard convection. They report improvements of more than 36% over existing methods on complex downstream tasks with limited data. These findings support CoDA-NO as a possible backbone for learning across multiphysics systems, with pretraining providing useful representations when downstream training examples are scarce.
neurips-2024-pretraining-codomain-attent.tldr: CoDA-NO uses attention over function channels to pretrain across PDE systems and improve learning on multiphysics tasks with limited data.

paragraphs: Human experts can guide Bayesian optimization by accepting or rejecting proposed query points. Their advice costs time and may be unreliable, so an optimizer needs to decide both how often to ask and how much to trust the answer. This paper develops an approach with theoretical guarantees addressing both decisions.

The handover guarantee bounds the cumulative number of expert labels sublinearly. Although early queries may require several labels, the required labeling effort asymptotically approaches zero. The no-harm guarantee adjusts trust using data so that the convergence rate is no worse than optimization without advice, even when advice is adversarial. This guarantee concerns convergence rate rather than every individual query outcome.

The trust adjustment avoids requiring a manually specified function to control confidence in experts. In battery-design applications involving human experts, the method outperforms existing baselines and remains robust across different labeling accuracies. The contribution is a principled way to benefit from expert knowledge while progressively reducing dependence on it and controlling the effect of unreliable recommendations.
neurips-2024-principled-bayesian-optimiz.tldr: The method incorporates expert accept/reject advice with guarantees on diminishing labeling effort and protection of the optimizer's convergence rate.

paragraphs: Time-varying linear state-space models describe complex neural signals through hidden variables with locally linear dynamics. Their appeal is mathematical interpretability, but existing estimation methods can be sensitive to dynamical noise and system nonlinearities. This sensitivity can produce inconsistent explanations for signals with similar dynamics, reducing their usefulness for scientific interpretation.

The paper introduces a probabilistic method for estimating latent variables in decomposed dynamical models. This change improves robustness to dynamical noise. The authors also extend the latent dynamics model to better handle nonlinear systems. Together, these contributions address both how hidden variables are inferred and how flexibly their evolution can be represented.

Evaluations on synthetic dynamical systems, including an empirically derived brain-computer interface experiment, show more accurate latent inference across nonlinear systems and varied noise conditions. On a clinical neurophysiology dataset, the method identifies coherent, interpretable structure that previous models do not recover. These results support more robust discovery of hidden neural dynamics while retaining the interpretability motivating this model family.
neurips-2024-probabilistic-decomposed-li.tldr: Probabilistic inference and an extended dynamics model improve the robustness of interpretable latent neural dynamics estimates.

paragraphs: Federated learning lets devices train together without sharing their underlying data, but individual updates can still expose information or carry poisoning attacks. Secure aggregation hides those updates while revealing their aggregate. This creates a conflict with defenses that need to inspect each participant's update in plaintext to assess whether it is harmful.

RFLPA combines robust aggregation with a secure aggregation protocol. It uses cosine similarity between local updates and server updates to guide aggregation. Verifiable packed Shamir secret sharing reduces communication, while a new dot-product aggregation algorithm addresses the increased information leakage involved in the computation. These components make the comparison-based defense compatible with protected updates.

The framework achieves a stated per-user communication cost of O(M+N). Experiments report reductions exceeding 75% in communication and computation overhead relative to BREA, a state-of-the-art secret-sharing method, while maintaining competitive accuracy. The results support the feasibility of combining poisoning defenses with secure aggregation at substantially lower overhead than that comparator in the evaluated settings.
neurips-2024-rflpa-a-robust-federated-le.tldr: RFLPA combines similarity-based poisoning defenses with secure aggregation while substantially reducing overhead relative to BREA in experiments.

paragraphs: A* search maintains an OPEN list of candidate nodes and uses heuristic values to decide which one to expand. SeeA* changes this selection process to encourage exploration. The motivation is that a heuristic can misjudge promising branches, especially when its predictions are insufficiently accurate, making strict reliance on its top-ranked choice inefficient.

At each selection, SeeA* constructs a dynamic subset of OPEN through selective sampling and expands the best-ranked node within that subset. Nodes with the strongest heuristic values are likely to be included, but they can occasionally be omitted. This creates opportunities to explore other branches while still making substantial use of the heuristic's guidance.

The paper compares three sampling techniques. Under an assumption about the distribution of prediction errors, it proves an efficiency advantage over A*, particularly with less accurate heuristics. Experiments on chemical retrosynthesis, integrated-circuit logic synthesis, and Sokoban also demonstrate efficiency against leading heuristic-search methods. The theoretical advantage is tied to the stated error-distribution assumption, while the experiments provide evidence across distinct search applications.
neurips-2024-seea-efficient-exploration-.tldr: SeeA* samples candidate nodes before selecting an expansion, improving exploration when heuristic guidance is imperfect.

paragraphs: Aligning a language model involves seeking useful responses while satisfying safety requirements. This paper expresses that goal as maximizing reward subject to a safety constraint. SACPO, its proposed algorithm, divides alignment into successive stages associated with the individual metrics, giving the constrained objective a practical stepwise training procedure.

The theoretical idea behind the method is that an optimal policy accounting for both reward and safety can be obtained directly from a policy already aligned for reward. SACPO builds on that relationship using alignment methods such as direct preference optimization. Its staged structure also permits flexibility in the algorithms and datasets used for the different metrics.

Under mild assumptions, the authors derive upper bounds on optimality and safety-constraint violation. These bounds characterize the method's behavior without asserting that every trained model has zero violations. Experiments with Alpaca-7B show better helpfulness and harmlessness than the state-of-the-art comparison method. The paper presents the approach as simple, stable, and computationally efficient for constrained language-model alignment.
neurips-2024-stepwise-alignment-for-cons.tldr: SACPO aligns language models in successive reward and safety stages, supported by conditional bounds and improved Alpaca-7B results.

paragraphs: Observational data and domain assumptions do not always determine a policy's effect uniquely. Unobserved confounding can leave several effects compatible with the available evidence, making a single causal estimate unjustified. This paper develops methods for bounding policy effects in these non-identifiable settings, using a causal graph together with observational data.

The authors provide graphical characterizations and derive analytical bounds for general probabilistic and conditional policies. Their bounds are tighter than existing results, narrowing the range of policy effects consistent with the evidence. This makes the uncertainty more informative while preserving the distinction between a bounded effect and an effect that can be uniquely identified.

The paper also develops a framework for estimating those bounds from finite samples, including higher-dimensional settings and continuously valued data. The estimators have favorable statistical properties, including fast convergence and robustness to model misspecification. Together, the analytical and estimation contributions support policy evaluation when causal uncertainty remains even after the available observations and structural assumptions are taken into account.
neurips-2024-towards-estimating-bounds-o.tldr: The paper derives tighter policy-effect bounds and estimators for observational settings where unobserved confounding prevents unique causal identification.

paragraphs: In a vision model's first layer, weight gradients depend directly on normalized pixel values. This gives image contrast and brightness a direct influence on update magnitudes: low-contrast images contribute less, while very bright or dark images can contribute more than moderately bright ones. TrAct changes how that first-layer update is constructed.

The method conceptually takes a gradient step on the representations produced by the first layer, creating proposed activation values. It then finds the first-layer weights whose outputs minimize squared distance to that proposal. The authors derive a closed-form solution and adapt it for robust stochastic training, allowing the procedure to be implemented efficiently.

Experiments report training speedups ranging from 1.25 to 4 times with only a small computational overhead. The authors demonstrate the approach with different optimizers and both convolutional and transformer vision architectures. These findings suggest that changing the first-layer update geometry can yield substantial training benefits without requiring discrete image inputs or replacing the vision model with an embedding-based input scheme.
neurips-2024-tract-making-first-layer-pr.tldr: TrAct constructs first-layer weight updates from proposed activation updates, accelerating training across tested vision models and optimizers.
